sentences.text: Kaijutitan is a genus of basal titanosaur dinosaur named after Japanese movie monsters, described by Filippi, Salgado, and Garrido in 2019. The only known species is Kaijutitan maui, and it belongs to the unranked family Titanosauria.

The holotype specimen, catalogued as MAU-Pv-CM-522, is a partial skeleton stored at the Museo Municipal Argentino Urquiza. This collection includes a skull, cervical and thoracic vertebrae, ribs, a sternum, shoulder girdle, arm bones, leg bones, and many indeterminate fragments.
The anterior cervical vertebrae possess bifid neural spines created by the backward convergence of a shelf from each parapophysis and the lower rib facet.
Kaijutitan lacks proximal pneumatopores in its dorsal ribs.
The proximal tibial condyle is narrow with its long axis oriented anteroposteriorly, while the upper surface of the tibia is narrow with its longitudinal axis directed from front to back.
The passage for the internal carotid artery is located posterior to the basipterygoid process, halfway between the basal tuberosities and the basipterygoid.

The back of the skull was surprisingly flattened vertically, and the occipital foramen was circular unlike the oval shape found in most related dinosaurs. The occiput was much wider than the base of the skull, suggesting the overall head was likely very wide. The anterior cervical vertebra, likely the third, was completely flattened.
Researchers estimate Kaijutitan's body weight was comparable to Giraffatitan and Notocolossus, between 38 and 60 tonnes. The estimated body length is between 25 and 30 meters.
The anterior cervical vertebrae feature a unique posterior keel created by the backward convergence of a shelf from each parapophysis and the lower rib facet.

Kaijutitan fossils were discovered in the Sierra Barrosa Formation near Rincón de los Sauces in Neuquén, Argentina, by researchers from two local museums. The skeleton of a large sauropod was discovered by technician Salvador Palomo in Cañadón Mistringa, Neuquén province, Argentina. Kaijutitan maui was named and described in 2019 by Leonardo Sebastián Filippi, Leonardo Salgado, and Carlos Alberto Garrido.

The holotype specimen was found in the upper Coniacian layer of the Sierra Barrosa Formation, dating to about 87 million years ago. The fossil skeleton was disarticulated and spread over an area of 20 square meters. Kaijutitan lived during the late Coniacian stage, approximately 87 million years ago.
Determining the body size of Kaijutitan is difficult because few vertebrae are preserved and the femur is incomplete.

Kaijutitan is classified as a basal titanosaurian, outside the Eutitanosauria clade, alongside Epachthosaurus. It is one of the most basal titanosaurs characterized by procoelic tail vertebrae. In 2019, Kaijutitan was the youngest known titanosaur with such a basal phylogenetic position. Kaijutitan belongs to the parent group Lithostrotia and is classified within the class Saurischia.

Kaijutitan lived during the Late Cretaceous Coniacian stage, approximately 89 to 86 million years ago, in what is now South America. The time range for Kaijutitan is estimated from 89.8 to 85.7 million years ago.
It is debated whether the bifurcated cervical spine process in Kaijutitan is a unique trait (autapomorphy) or a shared primitive trait, with authors assuming it evolved independently.
